items.followUp: Explain two ways biodiversity helps maintain the balance of an ecosystem.

rubric.why: Recognises that biodiversity helps maintain a balanced or stable ecosystem.
rubric.description: Biodiversity supports ecosystem balance and stability.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that biodiversity helps keep an ecosystem balanced or stable.

rubric.why: A variety of organisms form interconnected feeding relationships.
rubric.description: Different species form food chains and food webs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that biodiversity supports food chains or food webs.

rubric.why: Organisms contribute to recycling nutrients in ecosystems.
rubric.description: Biodiversity supports nutrient cycling.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking biodiversity with nutrient recycling.

rubric.why: A diverse ecosystem is better able to withstand or recover from changes.
rubric.description: Biodiversity increases ecosystem resilience to disturbances.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that biodiversity helps an ecosystem withstand or recover from disturbance.

rubric.why: A relevant example shows biodiversity's importance in a natural ecosystem.
rubric.description: Gives a relevant ecosystem example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable example, such as diverse forest species supporting food webs or animals pollinating plants.

modelAnswer: Biodiversity is the variety of living organisms in an ecosystem, and it helps maintain ecosystem balance and stability.
Different species are linked in food chains and food webs, so changes in one population can affect others.
A variety of organisms also supports essential processes such as nutrient cycling.
Biodiverse ecosystems are generally more resilient and can better withstand or recover from environmental changes.
For example, in a forest, many plant and animal species form food webs; insects pollinate plants, while decomposers recycle nutrients.

items.followUp: Describe how an increase in carbon dioxide concentration can affect photosynthesis, and state what happens when another factor becomes limiting.

rubric.why: Light provides energy for photosynthesis, and increasing its intensity raises the rate up to a limit.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of light intensity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that increasing light intensity increases the rate of photosynthesis up to a saturation point.

rubric.why: Carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis; more can raise the rate until another limit is reached.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of carbon dioxide concentration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that increasing carbon dioxide concentration increases the rate up to a limit.

rubric.why: Photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes, so temperature affects its rate.
rubric.description: Relates temperature to enzyme-controlled photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking temperature's effect on the rate to enzyme activity.

rubric.why: The rate does not increase indefinitely: temperature has an optimum, and other factors can limit the rate.
rubric.description: States the temperature limit or the limiting-factor principle.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the rate falls above the optimum temperature, or that another limiting factor prevents further increase.

modelAnswer: Increasing light intensity increases the rate of photosynthesis because light supplies the energy for the process; the rate levels off when another factor becomes limiting.
Increasing carbon dioxide concentration increases the rate because carbon dioxide is a raw material; the rate also levels off when another factor becomes limiting.
Increasing temperature raises the rate up to an optimum because photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes.
Above the optimum temperature, the rate decreases as the enzymes lose their proper functioning.

items.followUp: Explain what happens to a plant cell and an animal cell when they are placed in a hypotonic solution.

rubric.why: Water moves across the selectively permeable membrane by osmosis in response to the more concentrated external solution.
rubric.description: Explains the movement of water by osmosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that water leaves both cells by osmosis in a hypertonic solution.

rubric.why: An animal cell loses water and shrinks because it has no cell wall.
rubric.description: Describes the effect on the animal cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the animal cell shrinks or becomes crenated.

rubric.why: Water loss causes the plant cell's contents to contract away from the wall.
rubric.description: Describes plasmolysis in the plant cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the protoplast contracts or pulls away from the cell wall.

rubric.why: The plant cell wall is rigid and helps retain the cell's outer shape despite water loss.
rubric.description: Explains the role of the plant cell wall.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting that the wall remains in place or helps the plant cell retain its outer shape.

rubric.why: A labelled diagram should show the shrunken animal cell and plasmolysed plant cell in hypertonic solution, with water moving outward.
rubric.description: Provides a relevant labelled diagram.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a diagram showing both cell outcomes and outward water movement; accept a clearly labelled equivalent drawing.

modelAnswer: In a hypertonic solution, water leaves both plant and animal cells by osmosis.
The animal cell shrinks (crenates) because it has no cell wall to resist the loss of water.
In the plant cell, the protoplast loses water and contracts away from the cell wall; this is called plasmolysis.
The rigid cell wall remains in place and helps retain the plant cell's outer shape.
Diagram construction: draw an animal-cell circle 2 cm in diameter and a smaller, crenated outline inside it; label it “animal cell in hypertonic solution.”
Draw a plant-cell rectangle 4 cm long × 2.5 cm high; draw a smaller protoplast, about 2.5 cm × 1.2 cm, separated from the wall; label “cell wall,” “plasmolysed protoplast,” and “hypertonic solution.”
Draw at least two arrows pointing out of each cell and label them “water.”

items.followUp: Describe how the villi of the small intestine help in absorption.

rubric.why: Identifies the small intestine's position in the digestive tract.
rubric.description: States where the small intestine is located.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it lies between the stomach and large intestine.

rubric.why: Its length and coiling provide space and time for digestion and absorption.
rubric.description: Describes the small intestine's general structure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing it as a long or coiled tube.

rubric.why: Villi and microvilli increase the surface available for absorption.
rubric.description: Describes the absorptive lining.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning villi or microvilli and their increased surface area.

rubric.why: The small intestine completes digestion and absorbs digested food.
rubric.description: States the main functions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it completes digestion and/or absorbs digested nutrients.

modelAnswer: The small intestine is a long, coiled tube between the stomach and the large intestine.
Its inner lining has folds covered with many villi; the villi have microvilli that increase the surface area.
Digestive juices in the small intestine complete the digestion of food.
The digested nutrients are absorbed through the villi into the blood (and lymph).

items.followUp: What is a scientific theory, and how is it different from a hypothesis?

rubric.why: An observation is information obtained by watching or measuring.
rubric.description: Defines an observation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an observation is information gathered using senses or instruments.

rubric.why: A hypothesis is a proposed explanation that can be tested, unlike a direct observation.
rubric.description: Defines and distinguishes a hypothesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a hypothesis as a tentative, testable explanation based on observations.

modelAnswer: An observation is information gathered by using the senses or instruments to watch or measure something.
A hypothesis is a tentative, testable explanation proposed on the basis of observations.

items.followUp: What is turgidity, and how does a plant cell become turgid?

rubric.why: Turgor pressure is the pressure exerted by the cell contents against the cell wall.
rubric.description: Defines turgor pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying pressure exerted by the cell contents against the cell wall.

rubric.why: Water entering the cell increases pressure against the wall.
rubric.description: Links water entry to turgor pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that water entry by osmosis produces or increases this pressure.

modelAnswer: Turgor pressure is the pressure exerted by the cell contents against the cell wall.
It develops when water enters the cell by osmosis and the contents press against the wall.

items.followUp: State two functions of the nucleus.

rubric.why: The cytoplasm is where many of the cell's chemical reactions take place.
rubric.description: States that cytoplasm is a site of reactions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming metabolic or chemical reactions as a role of cytoplasm.

rubric.why: Cytoplasm holds cell organelles and can help substances move through the cell.
rubric.description: States a structural or transport role of cytoplasm.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that cytoplasm holds or supports organelles, or transports substances.

modelAnswer: Cytoplasm is the site of many metabolic and chemical reactions in the cell.
It holds and supports the cell organelles and helps transport substances within the cell.
